opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think if you ask ten roboticists that question you'll get ten different answers, but for me a few things stand out.

The first is generalization. We can now get robots to do some pretty impressive things in the lab: folding laundry, making coffee, assembling parts. But they tend to be brittle. Change the lighting, move the table, swap the mug for one with a different handle, and performance can fall apart. Humans don't have this problem. A child who learns to open one drawer can open almost any drawer. Getting that kind of robust, compositional generalization is, I think, the central challenge.

Closely tied to that is data. In language and vision we had the internet, billions of examples just sitting there. In robotics there's no equivalent. Every demonstration has to be collected on physical hardware, often by a human teleoperating the robot, which is slow and expensive. So a lot of my thinking, and my lab's work, is about how to get more out of less data. That means learning from human videos, using simulation, and designing representations and model structures that let skills transfer and recombine instead of being learned from scratch each time.

The third is long-horizon reasoning. Picking up an object is one thing. Cooking a meal is dozens of steps, with dependencies, failures, and recovery. A robot has to know what it's trying to achieve at a high level and also execute precise low-level motions, and errors compound over time. Bridging that gap between task planning and physical control is still very much open. I'm excited about combining the reasoning abilities of large models with more structured planning, but we're early.

And then there's the physical side people sometimes underestimate: contact-rich manipulation. Tasks like inserting a plug, tying a knot, or handling deformable objects depend heavily on force and touch, not just vision. Our sensing and our models of contact are still pretty crude compared to what a human hand does effortlessly.

So in short: generalization, data efficiency, long-horizon reasoning, and rich physical interaction. The exciting thing is that we're finally seeing real progress on all of them at once, and I think the next few years are going to be really interesting.

r001.rationale: The response names generalization, data efficiency, long-horizon reasoning, and contact-rich interaction as challenges, but it does not identify robots demonstrating physical common sense through their own manipulation as a particularly difficult problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the hardest problem isn't any single skill, it's generalization. We've gotten pretty good at getting a robot to do one task in one lab with one set of objects. The moment you change the lighting, swap the mug for a slightly different mug, or move the robot to a kitchen it has never seen, things fall apart in ways that would never trip up a human. So the real question is how you get a system that transfers its understanding across tasks, objects, and environments.

A big part of that comes down to data. In language and vision, the field could scrape the internet and get billions of examples essentially for free. Robotics doesn't have that. Every demonstration costs a human's time, and often a physical robot's time, and the data you collect is tied to a particular embodiment and setup. So a lot of the hardest work right now is figuring out where the data comes from. Can we learn from human video? Can we use simulation and actually close the gap to the real world? Can we build data collection pipelines that scale without needing an expert operator for every trajectory?

The second thing I'd point to is long-horizon reasoning. Picking up an object is one thing. Making a cup of coffee involves dozens of steps, each with its own failure modes, and the errors compound. If your low-level controller is ninety-five percent reliable, you're in bad shape after twenty steps. So we need systems that can plan over long horizons, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover. That ties into how we combine learned policies with structure, whether that's task decomposition, language, or some kind of world model that lets the robot anticipate the consequences of its actions.

And then there's contact. Manipulation is fundamentally about touching the world, and contact is discontinuous, hard to model, and hard to perceive. Deformable objects, tool use, anything with friction and force feedback, those are still very hard. Vision alone doesn't tell you how tight you're gripping or whether a plug is about to seat in a socket.

What's exciting is that these problems are starting to feel connected rather than separate. The foundation model era has given us a lot of new tools, but I think the robotics community has to be careful not to assume we can just borrow the recipe wholesale. The physical world pushes back in ways text never does.

r001.rationale: The response identifies generalization, data, long-horizon reasoning, and contact as hard problems, but does not identify robots demonstrating physical common sense through their own manipulation.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the hardest problems is generalization. We can get a robot to perform a particular task in a carefully controlled environment, but if you change the object, the lighting, or where things are placed, that same system can struggle. The challenge is getting robots to handle the variation that people barely notice.

Manipulation also involves contact, which makes it difficult to predict exactly what will happen. When you grasp something or slide it across a table, small differences in friction or geometry can matter a lot. A robot needs to use feedback continuously, recognize when something is going wrong, and adjust.

And then there’s the question of how we teach these capabilities at scale. Collecting robot experience takes time, and demonstrations don’t cover every situation. So how do we learn from limited experience and turn that into behavior that works reliably in new settings? I think that combination—generalization, feedback, and learning efficiently—is really central.

r001.rationale: The response describes generalization, contact feedback, and learning efficiently, but does not identify physical common sense demonstrated through a robot’s own manipulation as a particularly difficult problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the hardest problems is generalization. We can get a robot to do a particular task in a carefully controlled setting, but if you change the object, the lighting, or where things are placed, it can struggle. And in manipulation, those differences really matter: an object might look familiar but have a different weight or friction, so the robot has to adapt through interaction.

Another big challenge is data. For robots, collecting experience means physically doing things, which is slow, expensive, and sometimes risky. So how do we learn from demonstrations, simulation, and other sources of information, while still grounding that knowledge in what the robot can actually do?

And then there’s putting it all together over longer tasks. Making one successful grasp is very different from preparing a meal or cleaning up a kitchen. The robot needs to recognize when something went wrong, recover, and keep going. I think that combination of generalization, learning efficiently, and reliable recovery is where a lot of the hard work is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization, data efficiency, and recovery, and mentions adapting through interaction. It does not identify demonstrating physical common sense through a robot’s own manipulation as a particularly difficult problem.
